claims.text: High-temperature mechanical and thermoelastic behavior in the proposed refractory high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions modify short-range order.
Local lattice distortions and modified short-range order control defect nucleation.
Changes in dislocation behavior and thermal expansion produce a balance between high stiffness and improved ductility.
The initial refractory high-entropy alloy is homogeneous.
Adding compensating Hf increases atomic-scale lattice distortion.
Hf-induced lattice distortions disrupt local periodicity.
Disrupted local periodicity changes how dislocations initiate.
Disrupted local periodicity changes how dislocations propagate.
Hf-induced distortion modifies the elastic modulus relative to the baseline alloy.
Hf-induced distortion modifies thermal-expansion behavior relative to the baseline alloy.
Hf tuning enhances ductility without a critical compromise in stiffness.
Alloys with higher compensating Hf content will exhibit increased ductility relative to the baseline.
Alloys with higher compensating Hf content will exhibit modified stress-strain behavior relative to the baseline.
Alloys with higher compensating Hf content will exhibit altered elastic modulus and thermal-expansion coefficients relative to the baseline.
The effects of Hf tuning become more pronounced at high temperatures.
The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate near 70–90% of the melting temperature, where thermally activated dislocation processes are significant.
At lower temperatures, mechanisms other than the proposed distortion-mediated process may obscure or dominate the behavior.
